sections.heading: Contribution, profit and profitability
sections.body: Sales revenue is the value of sales recognised during a period. In a simple one-product situation, price multiplied by quantity gives sales revenue. Contribution is sales revenue less variable costs. It is used first to cover fixed costs; only contribution above fixed costs becomes profit. Profit is the revenue remaining after relevant costs have been deducted. Improving profitability can involve raising price, increasing volume, reducing variable or fixed costs, or improving the product mix, but the likely effect on demand, capacity and margins must be considered.

sections.heading: Contribution is not profit
sections.body: Contribution per unit is selling price per unit less variable cost per unit. Total contribution is the amount generated by all units to cover fixed costs and then profit. Profit takes account of fixed costs as well as variable costs. A business can therefore have positive contribution but make a loss if total contribution is lower than fixed costs. Revenue is also different from profit: a rise in revenue does not necessarily produce a rise in profit.

sections.heading: Identifying contribution correctly
sections.body: Example: a café sells a lunch for £12 and its ingredients and packaging cost £5 per lunch. Contribution per lunch is £7. This £7 is available towards rent, wages treated as fixed costs, and then profit. Non-example: calling the £7 profit. It is not profit unless the café has no fixed costs to cover. Similarly, a £1m rise in sales revenue is not automatically a £1m rise in profit.

sections.heading: Build total contribution step by step
sections.body: A UK clothing retailer sells 2,500 jackets at £48 each. Variable cost is £29 per jacket. First calculate contribution per unit: £48 minus £29 equals £19. Then multiply £19 by 2,500 units to find total contribution of £47,500. This is not yet profit: fixed costs must be deducted next. If variable cost rises while price stays unchanged, contribution per unit falls, so more units are needed to cover the same fixed costs.

sections.heading: Do not confuse output with break-even
sections.body: Selling more units normally raises total contribution when contribution per unit is positive, helping the business move towards or beyond break-even. However, the break-even output itself is driven by fixed costs and contribution per unit. A price reduction may increase output, but it also reduces contribution per unit unless variable costs fall too. The final effect on profit depends on whether the extra volume creates enough additional total contribution.

sections.heading: From price and costs to profit
sections.body: Selling price and demand influence output and sales revenue. Selling price less variable cost per unit gives contribution per unit. Contribution per unit multiplied by units sold gives total contribution. Total contribution first covers fixed costs; any excess can become profit. Therefore, higher variable costs without a matching price rise or productivity improvement compress contribution and may reduce profit. Changes in product mix can also change the overall margin because products can have different contribution levels.

sections.heading: Explain a profit-improvement decision
sections.body: A bakery is considering cutting the price of a popular cake to increase sales volume. Explain, in your own words, why the bakery should calculate the new contribution per cake and expected total contribution, rather than assuming that higher revenue will improve profit. Then identify one other factor, such as capacity, demand or cash timing, that should affect its decision.

sections.heading: Worked calculations: contribution
sections.body: A meal-kit business charges £36 per box and has a variable cost of £21 per box. Contribution per unit is £15. If it sells 3,200 boxes, total contribution is £48,000. This amount must cover fixed costs before it can be described as profit.

key_terms.definition: The value of sales recognised during a period.
The revenue figure presented for a period, which may include other income depending on the presentation.
Sales revenue less variable costs; it helps cover fixed costs and then profit.
Selling price per unit less variable cost per unit.
Contribution per unit multiplied by units sold.
A named profit or contribution measure expressed as a percentage of a stated comparable revenue or sales denominator.
Revenue less cost of sales under the applicable accounting presentation.
Profit from operations before financing and tax items under the relevant presentation.

worked_examples.scenario: A cinema sells a premium ticket for £18. The variable cost of servicing each ticket is £6.
steps: Identify the selling price per ticket as £18.
Identify the variable cost per ticket as £6.
Subtract variable cost per unit from selling price per unit.
Each ticket provides £12 towards fixed costs and then profit.

worked_examples.scenario: The cinema sells 2,750 premium tickets, each giving £12 contribution.
steps: Use the contribution per ticket of £12.
The result is total contribution, not automatically profit because fixed costs remain to be covered.

items.prompt: A sports shop sells a water bottle for £14. Its variable cost per bottle is £5. Calculate contribution per unit.
items.explanation: Contribution per unit is selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit: £14 − £5 = £9.

items.prompt: A florist earns contribution of £8 per bouquet and sells 1,850 bouquets. Calculate total contribution.
items.explanation: Total contribution equals contribution per unit multiplied by units sold: £8 × 1,850 = £14,800.

items.prompt: A small retailer has total contribution of £42,000 and fixed costs of £50,000. Compare its contribution with its profit position, and justify your answer.
items.answer: Contribution is positive at £42,000, but the retailer makes an £8,000 loss because contribution does not cover fixed costs.
items.explanation: Contribution is available to cover fixed costs first. As £42,000 is £8,000 below fixed costs of £50,000, no profit remains.

items.prompt: A gym plans to cut its monthly membership price. Explain one reason why this may fail to improve profit even if membership revenue rises.
items.answer: The lower price may reduce contribution per member, so the extra members may not generate enough additional contribution to cover fixed costs.
items.explanation: Revenue growth alone does not ensure profit growth. The gym must consider the change in contribution per member and the additional volume achieved.

items.prompt: Which statement is correct? A: Revenue and profit always rise by the same amount. B: Profit is always the same as cash held. C: Revenue can rise while profit falls if costs rise by more. Choose one.
items.explanation: Higher revenue can be outweighed by higher variable costs, fixed costs or both. Profit and cash also differ because accounting recognition and cash timing can differ.

items.prompt: Product A has a higher contribution margin than Product B, but Product B generates more total contribution. Give one valid interpretation.
items.answer: Product B may sell at a much higher volume, so its lower margin still produces more total contribution.
items.explanation: A margin is a relative percentage, whereas total contribution is an absolute amount. High margin can coexist with low total profit or contribution when volume is small.

items.prompt: A student says: 'A product sells for £30, has variable cost of £17 and fixed cost of £4 per unit, so contribution per unit is £9.' Identify and correct the error.
items.answer: The student wrongly subtracts fixed cost. Contribution per unit is £13: £30 − £17.
items.explanation: Contribution per unit uses only selling price and variable cost per unit. Fixed costs are covered afterwards by total contribution.

items.prompt: A manufacturer keeps its selling price unchanged but experiences an increase in variable cost per unit. Set out the likely chain of effects on contribution, break-even and profit.
items.answer: Contribution per unit falls; each sale covers less fixed cost; break-even output rises; and profit is likely to fall unless the business increases volume, raises price, cuts other costs or improves productivity.
items.explanation: Higher variable costs reduce the amount each unit contributes. With lower contribution per unit, more units are needed to cover the same fixed costs.

items.prompt: State the formula for contribution per unit and the formula for total contribution.
items.answer: Contribution per unit = selling price per unit − variable cost per unit. Total contribution = contribution per unit × units sold.
items.explanation: The first formula finds the contribution from one unit; the second scales that amount by sales volume.
